steps.title: No new rules — just new nouns
body: بِكَمْ هَذَا؟ ("how much is this?") is already something you can ask. Answering it just applies the counting rules you already know to a new kind of noun: money.

دُولَار (dollar), رِيَال (riyal), دِينَار (dinar), and جُنَيْه (pound) — four of the currencies you'll actually see across the Arab world — all count exactly like كِتَاب or أَخ or any other noun: 3-10 takes the plural, genitive (عَشَرَةُ دُولَارَاتٍ), 11-99 takes the singular, accusative (عِشْرُونَ دِينَارًا), and مِائَة takes a singular genitive noun the same way it always has.

steps.title: Ten dollars to a hundred riyals
steps.intro: Read the four currencies, then the three price sentences. Tap 🔊 to hear any line.

steps.title: Plural, or singular?
steps.prompt: Why دُولَارَاتٍ (plural) here, not a singular?

options.label: Ten follows the same 3-10 rule as any counted noun — plural, genitive
Prices always use plurals, no matter the number

steps.explanation: Nothing new here — عَشَرَةُ دُولَارَاتٍ follows the exact same 3-10 rule as عَشَرَةُ كُتُبٍ.

steps.title: Now singular?

options.label: Twenty follows the 11-99 rule — singular, accusative, same as any counted noun
Twenty is a special exception just for money

steps.explanation: Once the number passes ten, the counted noun switches to singular accusative — the same rule that already applies to عِشْرُونَ كِتَابًا.

steps.title: And a hundred?

options.label: مِائَة governs a genitive noun via iḍāfa, exactly as it does for any noun
A special price-only rule that only applies to مِائَة
رِيَال changes its spelling after مِائَة

steps.explanation: مِائَةُ رِيَالٍ works exactly like مِائَةُ كِتَابٍ — nothing about money changes the rule.

steps.title: You can talk about prices
steps.message: No new grammar this time — you just proved the counting rules you already know (3-10 plural, 11-99 singular, مِائَة's genitive) work for any noun at all, money included.
